text.p: Britain's economic recovery is being led by London which is racing ahead of the rest of the country with rising consumer spending set to prompt a mini-boom later this year, according to a report released on Wednesday.

Business Strategies Ltd, an independent research firm, said in its twice-yearly report Britain was flourishing on the back of rising incomes and windfall gains, but it was not heading for a 1980s-style boom.
"The UK is in for a good, but not outstanding year," said research director Neil Blake. "It's a mini-boom' and London is the star."

He said the forecast for growth in greater London in 1997 is well above the national average. "If achieved, the forecast of 4.2 percent growth will not be very far behind the 4.8 percent achieved in 1988 at the peak of the eighties boom."
The report followed a recent stream of strong UK economic data which has fed a pre-election war-of-words among British politicians.
BSL forecasts the economy overall will grow by 3.2 percent led by rapid expansion of service and communications sectors, and consumer spending as windfall gains materialise.
Conversion of four major UK building societies and the conclusion of personal equity plans means many Britons will receive hefty cash payouts in 1997.
"As well as continued bounceback from a deep recession, London is a major centre for fast growing industries and does particularly well in periods of fast consumer growth," BSL said.
The North of England is trailing badly behind the rest of Britain, the report said, dogged by weak growth in the manufacturing sector.
It said growth would slow to just 1.7 percent for 1997 in the northernmost part of England but, in general, a turnaround was expected in manufacturing output.

Blake denied the return of the north-south' divide in Britain, referring to the popular picture painted of the 1980s economic recovery where a grim, industrial northern wasteland contrasted with wealthy, booming towns in the south.
He noted that London had lost jobs in the financial services industry as companies relocated outside the city or introduced more advanced technology.
Relocation of service industries to the north has helped to balance troubled manufacturing firms, whose exports have suffered from sterling's recent strength.
The report assumed interest rates would hit at least seven percent by the end of this year, whichever way the May 1 election goes, which would put the brakes on growth beyond 1997.

Blake said he disagreed with British opposition Labour Party's recent pledge not to raise income taxes if the party beat the ruling Conservatives at the election. He said tax rises could prove more effective in controlling the strong economy than a rate hike.
Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke has so far resisted pressure from the Bank of England to raise rates, but analysts say high consumer spending growth will soon force the issue.
Although the report painted a bright economic picture for the short term, it said the robust growth could cause problems later on.

"A substantial slowdown in growth is likely to follow next year and the year after with higher interest rates and as the windfall gains effect drops out," said Business Strategies executive chairwoman Bridget Rosewell.
